meta.title: Who really said "To live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — John Henry Newman wrote it in his 1845 Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine. The Churchill version is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely John Henry Newman, from his 1845 Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine. Churchill later paraphrased it as 'To improve is to change.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Newman wrote this in ‘An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine’ (1845), Chapter 1, Section 1. The full sentence reads ‘…here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often.’ The popular short form is his genuine wording, confirmed against the primary text.

docMeta.dd: An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine

source.excerpt: It changes with them in order to remain the same. In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often.
trail: The exact sentence appears in Newman’s Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, Chapter 1 ↗, near the end of Section 1.
Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced section ↗, citing the 1845 Essay, Chapter 1, Section 1 (p. 39).
The famous Winston Churchill variant — ‘To improve is to change; to be perfect is to change often’ — is a later paraphrase; the Churchill Project traces it back to Newman as the original ↗.
source.excerptNote: Newman is describing how a living idea necessarily develops over time to stay true to itself — the ‘change’ he means is faithful growth, not reinvention.

author.name: John Henry Newman
author.heading: Who was John Henry Newman?
author.bio: John Henry Newman was a leading figure of the Oxford Movement who converted from the Church of England to Roman Catholicism in 1845 and was later made a cardinal. His Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, written as he moved toward Rome, argued that living ideas necessarily grow and change over time while remaining true to themselves. He was canonised as a saint by the Catholic Church in 2019.

misattribution.heading: The Churchill mix-up
misattribution.intro: This line is genuinely Newman’s, but it is often met in a punchier form credited to Winston Churchill.

items.why: The widely shared ‘To improve is to change; to be perfect is to change often’ is routinely pinned on Churchill. He did use a version of the thought, but the Churchill Project ↗ identifies Newman’s 1845 Essay as the real origin.

misattribution.truthLine: The original words are Newman’s, from his Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine ↗ (1845); the Churchill line is a later paraphrase of it.

context.heading: Why it was written
lead: Newman wrote the sentence at a hinge moment in his life. As he completed the Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine in 1845, he was reasoning his way out of the Church of England and into Roman Catholicism — and the book’s central claim is that a true doctrine, like a living thing, unfolds and grows over centuries rather than staying frozen.

In that setting the line is not a motivational slogan about self-improvement but a theological argument: to be a living idea in this world is to change, and the deepest fidelity shows itself through repeated, faithful development.
